title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 43–44
description: Advanced legal vocabulary and expressions, offences and court decisions; conflict, diplomacy, war and peace, and metaphorical warfare expressions.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from a user-supplied book. Vocabulary targets are based on the unit teaching pages, exercises and answer key; translations, example sentences and explanatory notes are independently written and do not reproduce textbook passages, exercise text or illustrations.

audit.scope: Units 43 and 44 teaching sections, crime/legal vocabulary and war and peace vocabulary, exercises 43.1–43.4 and 44.1–44.4, and relevant answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Selected short entries include conservative broad British IPA where reliable; long phrases have empty IPA rather than guessed connected-speech transcriptions.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations inside pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared teaching and exercise material with the book and answer key; wrote original examples and usage notes; checked legal meanings, conventional collocations, plural/countability, provenance, spelling, unique IDs, JSON schema and word/sentence audio separation.
audit.limitations: The package has no MP3 recordings. Browser import, TTS output and live speech recognition have not been tested. Legal terms follow the source’s predominantly British-English context, and precise legal classifications and procedures can differ by jurisdiction.

units.title: Unit 43 — The letter of the law
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 43. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Society and institutions · law, legal procedures and offences
learningObjectives: Distinguish legal decisions such as uphold, overturn, quash, annul and amend, and use their typical objects.
Recognise formal legal verbs and related nouns, including infringement, allegation and impeachment.
Describe offences and offender terms accurately, with appropriate caution about differing legal systems.
Use fixed idioms with law while distinguishing figurative meanings from legal terminology.

sectionsChecked: A, B and C teaching sections including labelled vocabulary, examples, and definitions

items.example: The official was accused of bending the law to speed up the approval.
items.note: Suggests stretching legal rules, often while claiming not to break them outright; not a legal defence.

items.pt: infringir uma lei; contrariar uma disposição legal
items.example: The proposed arrangement could contravene a law protecting consumer data.
items.note: Formal verb; contravene a regulation or the terms of an agreement.

items.example: The company was investigated for a contravention of environmental regulations.
items.note: Formal noun; commonly in contravention of a law, order or agreement.

items.example: The new policy may infringe workers' rights to privacy.
items.note: Infringe is common with rights, laws and rules; usually infring(e) on a right in some varieties, especially US English.

items.example: The court considered whether the copying constituted an infringement of copyright.
items.note: Common construction: an infringement of rights or rules; it is also a legal term in intellectual property.

items.pt: iniciar processo de impeachment contra um presidente
items.example: Legislators voted to impeach the president over alleged misconduct.
items.note: Impeachment is a formal charge or constitutional procedure; it does not automatically mean removal from office.

items.pt: impeachment; processo formal de responsabilização política
items.example: The impeachment proceedings attracted international attention.
items.note: Refers to formal proceedings against a public officeholder; exact procedure differs across jurisdictions.

items.example: Her solicitor advised her to lodge an appeal before the deadline.
items.note: British legal collocation for officially submitting an appeal against a ruling.

items.example: The defendant intends to appeal against the sentence.
items.note: Appeal is both a noun and verb; appeal against is common in British English.

items.pt: manter uma decisão judicial; confirmar um veredito
items.example: The higher court upheld the original verdict after reviewing the evidence.
items.note: Means confirm a previous decision as valid; contrasts with overturn.

items.pt: reverter um veredito; reformar uma decisão
items.example: The appeal court overturned the verdict because crucial evidence was excluded.
items.note: Means reverse a previous judicial decision; contrasts with uphold.

items.pt: obstruir a justiça; interferir ilicitamente no andamento da justiça
items.example: Hiding evidence could amount to perverting the course of justice.
items.note: Established legal expression in some jurisdictions, particularly Britain, for improperly obstructing justice.

items.pt: desvirtuamento da justiça; obstrução da justiça
items.example: The deliberate destruction of records was described as a perversion of justice.
items.note: Formal nominal form used to criticise serious interference with justice; precise legal charges vary.

items.example: The appellate court quashed the conviction after finding serious procedural errors.
items.note: Quash means set aside an official decision, particularly a conviction; not simply reduce a penalty.

items.example: The wrongful conviction was reviewed years after the trial.
items.note: In legal usage, a finding of guilt; elsewhere conviction can mean a firmly held belief.

items.example: The ruling may set a precedent for future privacy disputes.
items.note: A prior ruling can guide later cases, especially in common-law legal systems.

items.pt: precedente; decisão anterior que orienta casos futuros
items.example: The judge examined a relevant precedent before issuing the judgment.
items.note: Pronunciation and weight of precedent vary by legal system; not every prior decision is binding.

items.pt: atribuir guarda de uma criança por decisão judicial
items.example: The court awarded custody to the child's father after a detailed assessment.
items.note: Used when a court formally gives parental or legal responsibility; practice and terminology vary by jurisdiction.

items.example: The judge granted custody to the aunt pending a further hearing.
items.note: Often interchangeable with award custody in general accounts; custody can also mean detention in other contexts.

items.example: The judge annulled the marriage after reviewing the legal grounds.
items.note: An annulment declares a marriage invalid under relevant legal rules; distinct from divorce.

items.example: The application for annulment was considered separately from divorce proceedings.
items.note: Noun from annul; a marriage or agreement may be annulled.

items.pt: processar alguém judicialmente; ajuizar ação contra alguém
items.example: The customer threatened to sue the company over a faulty product.
items.note: Usually a civil action seeking a legal remedy; sue someone for damages or negligence.

items.example: Investigators allege that several payments were concealed from auditors.
items.note: A legal or journalistic verb indicating a claim not yet established as fact.

items.example: The newspaper clearly labelled the statements as allegations.
items.note: An allegation must not be reported as a proven finding.

items.example: Parliament proposed to amend the law to clarify the reporting requirements.
items.note: Amend means officially change part of a law rather than repeal it entirely.

items.example: The committee approved an amendment to the draft legislation.
items.note: Common collocation: propose, table or adopt an amendment.

items.example: The tribunal examined evidence of discrimination during the recruitment process.
items.note: Treatment that unfairly disadvantages someone on a protected ground; legislation differs by place.

items.pt: discriminar; tratar alguém de modo desigual
items.example: Employers must not discriminate against candidates on the basis of age.
items.note: This negative sense normally takes against someone or a group.

items.pt: apropriação indevida; desvio de recursos sob responsabilidade de alguém
items.example: An internal audit uncovered embezzlement of the organisation's funds.
items.note: Misappropriation of money entrusted to a person, typically through work.

items.pt: desviar recursos confiados à própria administração
items.example: The accountant was convicted of attempting to embezzle client money.
items.note: Verb for misappropriating entrusted funds, not a general synonym for steal.

items.pt: autor de desvio de recursos; pessoa que comete apropriação indevida
items.example: Prosecutors accused the former treasurer of acting as an embezzler.
items.note: A person who embezzles money or property entrusted to them.

items.example: The employer adopted stricter procedures for reporting workplace harassment.
items.note: Repeated unwanted or intimidating conduct; exact legal definitions vary.

items.example: The manager was accused of harassing junior employees.
items.note: Verb related to harassment; harass someone, not harass to someone.

items.pt: negociação de valores mobiliários com uso indevido de informação privilegiada
items.example: Regulators investigated suspected insider trading before the merger announcement.
items.note: Financial-market expression; dealing is a common British alternative.

items.example: The regulator imposed penalties for unlawful insider dealing.
items.note: British-English term commonly used alongside insider trading.

items.pt: pessoa que negocia usando informação privilegiada ilegalmente
items.example: The report described how the insider trader profited from confidential information.
items.note: The wrong depends on unlawful use of non-public price-sensitive information.

items.example: The investigation focused on money laundering through shell companies.
items.note: Concealing or disguising the illegal origins of funds.

items.example: The suspects allegedly used false invoices to launder money.
items.note: Fixed verb + noun collocation for disguising illicit funds.

items.pt: pessoa que pratica lavagem de dinheiro
items.example: Police identified a suspected money launderer within the network.
items.note: Agent noun for a person who launders illegal proceeds.

items.example: The witness was investigated for possible perjury after contradicting sworn evidence.
items.note: A knowingly false statement under oath in a legally relevant context; not every inaccurate statement is perjury.

items.example: A witness who knowingly lies under oath may commit perjury.
items.note: The fixed collocation uses commit, not make, perjury.

items.pt: pessoa que presta falso testemunho sob juramento
items.example: The prosecutor argued that the key witness was a perjurer.
items.note: Agent noun from perjury; uncommon outside formal legal reporting.

items.example: She reported repeated unwanted messages as part of a pattern of stalking.
items.note: Persistent unwanted attention or monitoring; often involves threats or fear.

items.example: The former colleague was accused of stalking the complainant.
items.note: The verb takes a direct object: stalk someone.

items.pt: perseguidor obsessivo; pessoa que pratica stalking
items.example: The victim recognised the stalker near the office.
items.note: Agent noun; avoids implying that every isolated contact constitutes a crime.

items.pt: entrada não autorizada em propriedade alheia; invasão de terreno
items.example: The landowner warned visitors that entering the enclosed field could be trespass.
items.note: In England, ordinary trespass is often a civil wrong rather than necessarily a criminal offence.

items.pt: invasor de propriedade; pessoa sem permissão para entrar
items.example: A trespasser had crossed the fence after the site was closed.
items.note: Someone who enters land without permission; criminal status depends on circumstances and law.

items.example: She described herself as a law-abiding resident who had never been fined.
items.note: Usually placed before a noun, as in law-abiding citizen; does not mean a person working in law.

items.example: The campaign promised tougher measures against repeat law-breakers.
items.note: Someone who breaks the law, especially repeatedly or deliberately.

items.word: take the law into your own hands
items.pt: fazer justiça com as próprias mãos
items.example: The community leader urged residents not to take the law into their own hands.
items.note: Means attempting punishment outside the lawful process.

items.pt: ditar regras de modo autoritário; impor sua vontade
items.example: On her first day, the new supervisor began laying down the law.
items.note: Idiom for strongly telling people what is permitted, not necessarily making actual legislation.

items.pt: pessoa que age segundo as próprias regras
items.example: The brilliant but unpredictable consultant is a law unto himself.
items.note: Usually be a law unto oneself; yourself, himself or herself changes with the subject.

units.title: Unit 44 — War and peace
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 44. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Society and institutions · conflict, diplomacy and war metaphors
learningObjectives: Describe conflict escalation, civil unrest, violence and the impact on civilians with precise terminology.
Discuss diplomacy, sanctions, military action, interventions, ceasefires and peacekeeping.
Use war-related verbs and collocations such as wage war, besiege, ambush and monitor a ceasefire.
Recognise metaphors of warfare used in political, commercial and everyday language.

sectionsChecked: A, B and C teaching sections including labelled vocabulary, examples, and definitions

items.pt: último recurso; medida tomada quando as demais falharam
items.example: The negotiators treated military force as a last resort.
items.note: Usually as a last resort; used when all other realistic options have failed.

items.example: Weeks of quiet diplomacy helped reopen the negotiations.
items.note: Actions and negotiations through which governments manage international relations.

items.example: The regional organisation introduced economic sanctions following the treaty violation.
items.note: Restrictions intended to influence a state's conduct; often impose or lift sanctions.

items.example: Ministers debated whether to take military action without a wider coalition.
items.note: General collocation for using military force, not identical to formally declaring war.

items.example: The military operation was suspended while talks continued.
items.note: A planned action carried out by armed forces.

items.example: The report compared the sophistication of weaponry used by different forces.
items.note: Collective uncountable noun: modern weaponry, not weaponries.

items.example: Analysts questioned whether hi-tech weaponry would reduce civilian harm.
items.note: A combination describing technologically advanced weapons; weaponry is uncountable.

items.example: Aid organisations documented civilian casualties after the attack.
items.note: Casualties include people injured as well as killed; avoid equating it with deaths only.

items.example: The resolution called for an assessment of the possible consequences of military intervention.
items.note: Organised involvement by armed forces in a situation or another territory.

items.example: Mediators credited the intervention with preventing further escalation.
items.note: The noun of intervene; can also describe non-military action.

items.example: The proposed strategy was openly described as an attempt at regime change.
items.note: The removal or replacement of a government or governing system, sometimes by force.

items.example: The novel depicts life under a tyrannical regime.
items.note: Describes cruel and oppressive exercise of power.

items.example: The movement sought to overthrow the dictatorship.
items.note: Overthrow means remove from power, often by force; past tense overthrew, past participle overthrown.

items.example: A prolonged civil war displaced millions of residents.
items.note: A war between groups within the same country.

items.example: Months of civil unrest preceded the negotiations.
items.note: Public disturbances, protests or disorder, not necessarily full-scale civil war.

items.example: Clashes between rival groups disrupted the peace talks.
items.note: Can be physical fights or strong disputes; commonly clashes between groups.

items.example: Rival political factions signed a temporary agreement.
items.note: As an adjective before a noun or as a noun; rival factions/groups.

items.example: The agreement recognised the linguistic rights of several ethnic communities.
items.note: Refers to shared cultural, linguistic or ancestral identity; not an automatic synonym for racial.

items.example: The dispute could escalate if neither side agrees to talks.
items.note: Often escalate into something more serious or escalate tensions.

items.pt: guerra total; conflito de grande escala
items.example: A series of border incidents developed into all-out war.
items.note: All-out means complete or unrestricted in scale or intensity.

items.example: The inquiry documented brutal treatment of detained civilians.
items.note: Strong adjective for extreme violence or cruelty.

items.example: Human rights groups condemned the suppression of peaceful demonstrations.
items.note: Can describe forceful prevention of activity or expression; here, often brutal suppression.

items.pt: limpeza étnica; expulsão violenta de uma população
items.example: Investigators documented allegations of ethnic cleansing in the border region.
items.note: A grave expression for forcibly removing an ethnic group from an area, commonly through violence.

items.pt: massacre; assassinato de grande número de pessoas
items.example: Witnesses described a massacre of villagers during the conflict.
items.note: Deliberate killing of many people, especially defenceless civilians.

items.example: Local mediators supported a long-term process of conflict resolution.
items.note: Measures to address disputes and find an enduring settlement.

items.example: Decades of mistrust made the negotiations unusually fragile.
items.note: Lack of trust, often between communities or institutions.

items.example: The reconciliation programme tried to address years of mutual hatred.
items.note: Strong noun derived from hate; hatred of or towards a group.

items.pt: travar guerra; conduzir campanha de guerra
items.example: The two kingdoms waged war over control of the valley.
items.note: Wage war on or against an opponent; figuratively wage war on a social problem.

items.example: Negotiators called for an immediate end to hostilities.
items.note: Usually plural; active fighting or military confrontation.

items.example: Both armies agreed to cease hostilities at dawn.
items.note: Cease is a formal alternative to stop; hostilities is normally plural.

items.example: Relief workers called for an end to the bloodshed.
items.note: Uncountable noun describing violent killing and injury.

items.example: Enemy forces besieged the city for several weeks.
items.note: Besiege means surround and attack over time; noun siege.

items.example: The prolonged siege left the city short of food and medicine.
items.note: Military encirclement of a town or stronghold; also figurative in under siege.

items.example: The convoy survived an ambush on a mountain road.
items.note: Noun or verb for an unexpected attack from concealed positions.

items.example: The patrol was ambushed while returning to its base.
items.note: Passive form common in reports of military attacks.

items.example: The two factions agreed to a three-day truce.
items.note: A negotiated pause in fighting, not necessarily a lasting peace settlement.

items.pt: cessar-fogo; acordo de suspensão dos ataques
items.example: Monitors reported several violations of the ceasefire.
items.note: A formal or informal halt in fighting; may be temporary or longer term.

items.example: The government declared a ceasefire before the peace conference.
items.note: Common formal collocation; declaring a ceasefire does not guarantee compliance.

items.example: An international peacekeeping force was deployed to monitor the buffer zone.
items.note: Personnel deployed to help maintain peace, often under an international mandate.

items.example: International observers recorded developments near the border.
items.note: Independent or external people monitoring a process or agreement.

items.pt: monitorar o cumprimento de um cessar-fogo
items.example: Neutral observers were appointed to monitor the ceasefire.
items.note: Monitor means observe and report compliance, not directly enforce the agreement.

items.example: The rebels entered negotiations after months of fighting.
items.note: People resisting or fighting against an established authority; context determines legal classification.

items.example: The rebellion spread from the northern region to several towns.
items.note: Collective action opposing established authority, sometimes involving armed force.

items.example: The military campaign continued through the winter.
items.note: A planned series of military actions, not necessarily a single battle.

items.pt: autor de atentado suicida com explosivos
items.example: Police reported that a suicide bomber had targeted the checkpoint.
items.note: An attacker who detonates explosives and intentionally dies in the attack.

items.pt: combater intensamente um problema; declarar guerra figurada
items.example: The city pledged to wage war on illegal dumping.
items.note: Figurative extension of wage war; be cautious with militaristic rhetoric in formal writing.

items.example: Reporters besieged the actor outside the courthouse.
items.note: Figurative meaning: crowd around someone with demands or questions, rather than a literal military siege.

items.example: The firm launched an advertising campaign for its new service.
items.note: Campaign extends from coordinated military activity to a planned series of promotional actions.

items.example: Three startups are battling to win the research contract.
items.note: Figurative verb often used for intense competition; battle to achieve a goal.

items.pt: domínio de mercado; posição de liderança predominante
items.example: The manufacturers competed for market supremacy in electric vehicles.
items.note: Supremacy means dominant position; common with battle for market supremacy.

items.word: have a fight on your hands
items.pt: ter uma batalha difícil pela frente
items.example: The campaigners have a fight on their hands to preserve the old library.
items.note: Idiom meaning face a difficult struggle to achieve a result.

items.example: A fleet of official vehicles carried the delegates to the summit.
items.note: Fleet originally refers to ships and extends to multiple cars, lorries or aircraft.

items.example: Officials travelled in bullet-proof cars during the visit.
items.note: Literally resistant to bullets; figuratively describes a robust plan or argument.
